bib.title: Can Large Language Models Reason and Plan?

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "Can Large Language Models Reason and Plan?", Subbarao Kambhampati (Arizona State University), arXiv:2403.04121v2 (8 Mar 2024). The text says a version appears in the Annals of the New York Academy of Sciences. It is a short perspective piece, not an empirical paper.

COVERAGE: 19,885 of 19,885 chars read, which is all 5 of 5 pages. Nothing was skipped. The references are listed in the text, and there are no appendices.

CLAIMS
(The paper has almost no new numbers of its own. All of its quantitative content is in the first claim. The remaining claims are qualitative arguments.)

- Claim: GPT-4 reached about 30% accuracy on Blocks World planning, and GPT-3 to GPT-3.5 to GPT-4 showed modest improvement. Accuracy was lower in other domains.
  number: 30%
  setup: Planning instances derived from International Planning Competition domains, including Blocks World. Models were GPT-3, GPT-3.5 and GPT-4, tested by the author's group in 2022-2023. The paper gives no instance counts or prompt details. These come from refs 12 and 13 and were not read.
  quote: "Initial results showed that there was some improvement in the accuracy of generated plans from GPT3 to GPT3.5 to GPT4, with GPT4 reaching 30% empirical accuracy in the Blocks World (albeit still lower in other domains)."
  where: p.2

- Claim: When action and object names were obfuscated, GPT-4's planning performance dropped sharply. This is evidence that its gains came from approximate retrieval and not from planning. Off-the-shelf AI planners were unaffected.
  number: none ("plummeted precipitously"; no figure given)
  setup: PlanBench-style test domains (refs 11, 12) with names obfuscated. No figure is given in this paper.
  quote: "GPT4's empirical performance plummeted precipitously, despite the fact that none of the standard off-the-shelf AI planners have any trouble with such obfuscation."
  where: p.2

- Claim: LLMs are best seen as "universal approximate retrieval" (n-gram models on steroids) and not as principled reasoners. They are described as a "giant non-veridical memory", an external System 1.
  number: GPT-3.5 is described as "a roughly 3001-gram model"
  setup: Conceptual argument, no experiment.
  quote: "GPT3.5 that powered the original ChatGPT is, for example, a roughly 3001-gram model of language."
  where: p.1, footnote

- Claim: Self-critique and self-verification do not reliably help. In the author's lab's studies, performance got worse because the LLM hallucinated both false positives and false negatives when verifying its own outputs. The belief that verifying is easier than generating (NP-style reasoning) does not carry over to LLMs.
  number: none
  setup: Two studies from the author's lab, on plan verification (ref 10) and constraint verification (ref 9). Details were not read.
  quote: "Indeed two recent studies from my lab–one on plan verification10 and the other on constraint verification 9–seem to throw cold water on this optimism by showing that with “self-verification” performance actually worsens. This is because LLMs hallucinate both false positives and false negatives while verifying the solutions they generate."
  where: p.3

- Claim: Self-improvement claims in earlier literature tend to come from tacit-knowledge tasks, such as essay writing. Those tasks have no sound verifier, so a bad critic is hard to detect.
  number: none
  quote: "One reason this is not recognized in earlier literature is that there self-verification claims are often made in the context of tacit knowledge tasks for which there is little possibility of a verifier"
  where: p.3

- Claim: The recommended pattern is LLM-Modulo (generate, test, critique). The LLM proposes candidates, and an external sound, model-based verifier does the back-prompting and certifies the final answer.
  number: none
  setup: Position and framework from ref 6 (Kambhampati et al. 2024, arXiv 2402.01817). It is not evaluated in this paper.
  quote: "The cleanest approach–one we advocate12,6–is to let an external model-based plan verifier do the back prompting and to certify the correctness of the final solution."
  where: p.2

- Claim: Human-in-the-loop iterative prompting is vulnerable to the Clever Hans effect. A human who knows the right answer steers the LLM, so the credit for correct results belongs to the human. The approach is of doubtful relevance when the human cannot verify the answer.
  number: none
  quote: "it is highly susceptible to the Clever Hans effect, where the LLM is merely generating guesses, and it is the human in the loop, with the knowledge of right vs. wrong solutions, who is steering the LLM"
  where: p.3

- Claim: Fine-tuning on planning instances did not give significant improvement in the author's limited experiments. The author argues it would only convert planning into memory-based retrieval anyway.
  number: none
  quote: "While our own limited experiments didn’t show any significant improvement through fine tuning"
  where: p.2

- Claim: Many papers claiming LLM planning confuse general planning knowledge with executable plans. They either work in domains where subgoal interactions can be ignored, or they leave interaction resolution to humans who repeatedly correct the plan. Planning needs (a) domain knowledge and (b) assembling it into a plan that handles subgoal and resource interactions.
  number: none
  setup: The author's examination of several papers (ref 7, a tutorial). The paper does not name them.
  quote: "Many of the papers claiming planning abilities of LLMs, on closer examination, wind up confusing general planning knowledge extracted from the LLMs for executable plans."
  where: p.4

- Claim: LLMs are useful as approximate sources of world-model and preference knowledge. Humans or critics verify and refine this knowledge and hand it to model-based solvers. LLMs take the place of the "knowledge engineer".
  number: none
  setup: Ref 1 (Guan et al., NeurIPS 2023).
  quote: "LLMs can be a rich source of approximate models of world/domain dynamics and user preferences, as long as the humans (and any specialized critics) in the loop verify and refine the models, and give them over to model-based solvers."
  where: p.4

- Claim: The same logic applies to code generation. LLMs help as co-pilots, but nothing guarantees the code is correct. Utility is helped by higher-quality GitHub training data and by interpreters in the loop catching syntax errors.
  number: none
  quote: "there is never any guarantee that the code they generate is correct."
  where: p.5, footnote

- Claim: The conclusion is that nothing the author has seen shows LLMs do reasoning or planning as normally understood. Their idea generation is valuable, but it needs external checking.
  number: none
  quote: "nothing that I have read, verified, or done gives me any compelling reason to believe that LLMs do reasoning/planning, as normally understood."
  where: p.4

LIMITS
- The paper is an opinion and perspective piece. It reports no tables, no instance counts, no confidence intervals and no ablations. The one number (30%) is a single headline figure taken from earlier work.
- The evidence is the author's own group's tests, on PDDL-style classical planning (Blocks World, IPC domains) with GPT-3, GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 in 2022-2023. It says nothing about later reasoning models. That is a clear way the evidence has dated. The text itself predates o1-style models and any RL-trained tool-calling.
- The author concedes that fine-tuning with more data and effort might improve the quality of LLM guesses. He also concedes that humans can sometimes self-correct, and that seeing patterns is valuable ("not anything to be sneezed at").
- The self-verification result is stated for plan and constraint verification only. It is not shown for all tasks.
- The paper does not say how LLM-Modulo performs in practice. It points to ref 6.

BUILDS ON
- Kahneman 2011, Thinking, Fast and Slow (System 1 / System 2).
- Valmeekam et al. 2022 and 2023 (planning benchmark, "On the planning abilities of large language models - a critical investigation", PlanBench).
- Valmeekam, Marquez and Kambhampati 2023 (self-critiquing plans), and Stechly, Marquez and Kambhampati 2023 (GPT-4 doesn't know it's wrong).
- Kambhampati et al. 2024, LLM-Modulo (arXiv 2402.01817).
- Guan et al. 2023 (LLMs as world-model builders for planning).
- Kambhampati 2021, "Polanyi's revenge and AI's new romance with tacit knowledge".
- Pólya, How to Solve It (mentioned in the text).
- Kugel and Hiltner, New York Times 2023 (AI-generated travel guidebooks).

CODE: none.

FIGURES (not extracted with the script; the captions come from the text)
- Fig. 1 (p.1): the LLM as a giant external non-veridical memory, a pseudo System 1. It shows the fine-tuning route as compiling System 2 into System 1.
- Fig. 2 (p.3): xkcd-style graphic showing that claimed reasoning is often subconscious human iterative prompting (Clever Hans).
- Fig. 3 (p.4): the LLM as an approximate knowledge source trained over civilizational knowledge, in the role of knowledge engineer.

PROBLEMS
- The extraction was clean text with no embedded instructions.
- The figure contents were not seen, only their captions.
- Relevance to the target note (01-agent-fundamentals.md), for the calling session to decide. The note's sources list has no Kambhampati entry. Its "Pitfalls" bullet "Trusting the model's own explanation" and its "Treating 'the agent said it finished' as success" bullet, together with the reflection-error row of Huyen's failure table and the "compute what can be computed" rule, are in line with this paper's argument. The paper's claims on self-verification (p.3) and on external verifiers (p.2) sharpen those points. The note's wording "the model should be checked against it" matches LLM-Modulo. I did not check the note against its other sources.
